title: Arrays in Clinic and Court: AmpliChip, Myriad and Exosome miRNA
summary: Meet the first clinical microarray (the AmpliChip CYP450 pharmacogenetic test), learn what the 2013 AMP v. Myriad ruling decided about patenting isolated DNA and cDNA, and see why exosomes and their microRNA cargo are studied as a liquid-biopsy source.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 70 Hits 2 (Roche AmpliChip as the first cleared microarray device), 3 (2013 AMP v. Myriad) and 14 (exosomes as a biomarker source; ovarian cancer exosomal miRNA). Checked against Samer 2013, Moyer 2025, Li 2008, Lemuth 2015, Dodgen 2013, Zhou 2020, Doyle 2019 and Hannafon 2013 (Europe PMC full text), the Taylor 2008 abstract (full text not open access) and the Supreme Court opinion text on the Cornell LII site. The FDA 510(k) database pages for the AmpliChip could not be retrieved (HTTP 404 via the session proxy), so the clearance year is given as “mid-2000s” (reviews say 2004 or 2005). Hit 3 is US law; Philippine patent rules are not covered (register flag proposed). Hit 14: exosome size bands and naming vary (ISEV prefers “extracellular vesicles”) and the ovarian cancer finding is a single 2008 study (register flag proposed). Not taught: Affymetrix density and the >400 features/cm² patent line (Hit 5, Trap 3) and nylon macroarray autofluorescence (Hit 9, Trap 1), for which no readable open source was found.

objectives: Identify the AmpliChip CYP450 test as the first clinical microarray and state which genes it genotypes.
State what the 2013 AMP v. Myriad decision held about isolated natural DNA and cDNA, and what it left undecided.
Describe exosomes, their cargo and why they are studied as a liquid-biopsy source.

scenes.title: Three proposals, one meeting
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a molecular laboratory’s planning meeting hears three proposals — (1) a psychiatry clinic wants CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 genotyping on a microarray before antidepressant dosing; (2) a start-up says it will patent the isolated, naturally occurring BRCA1 sequence it uses as a probe; (3) a researcher wants to profile microRNA in blood exosomes to tell ovarian cancer from benign disease. Question token: “Which of these hold up?”

cues.text: Invented scenario. A molecular lab hears three proposals: genotype two drug-metabolising genes on a microarray before dosing, and patent an isolated, natural BRCA1 sequence.
The third: profile microRNA carried in blood exosomes to tell ovarian cancer from benign disease.
Which of these proposals hold up, scientifically and legally?

scenes.title: The first clinical array: AmpliChip CYP450
scenes.altText: Schematic chip card: the Roche AmpliChip CYP450 test, developed by Roche Molecular Systems with Affymetrix, is an oligonucleotide microarray hybridisation assay that genotypes CYP2D6 and CYP2C19. Reviews describe it as the first clinically available microarray-based tool and the first FDA-approved pharmacogenetic test (market approval reported as 2004 in one review, 2005 in another). Workflow card: PCR amplification, labelling, hybridisation to the chip, scanning, and software that predicts the metaboliser phenotype. Limits card: it does not determine the exact number of extra CYP2D6 copies; phenotype prediction was strongest for poor metabolisers; one South African cohort had a high assay failure rate.

cues.text: The first microarray to become clinically available was a pharmacogenetic chip: the Roche AmpliChip CYP450 test, built on Affymetrix technology.

It genotypes two cytochrome P450 genes, CYP2D6 and CYP2C19, which help metabolise roughly a quarter of prescription drugs. Reviews call it the first FDA-approved pharmacogenetic test, from the mid-2000s.
The DNA is amplified by PCR, labelled, and hybridised to oligonucleotide probes on the chip. The chip is scanned, and software predicts the metaboliser phenotype from the genotype.
Its limits: it cannot count exactly how many extra CYP2D6 copies are present, phenotype prediction was best for poor metabolisers, and one South African study reported frequent assay failures.

scenes.title: Who can own a gene? AMP v. Myriad (2013)
scenes.altText: Ruling card (US Supreme Court, Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics, decided June 13, 2013): a naturally occurring DNA segment is a product of nature and is not patent eligible merely because it has been isolated. cDNA card: cDNA is patent eligible because it is not naturally occurring — it is an exons-only molecule made in the laboratory — except that a very short cDNA with no introns removed may be indistinguishable from natural DNA. Not-decided card: method claims, new applications of knowledge about BRCA1/BRCA2, and DNA with an altered nucleotide order were not at issue. Scope token: US law only.

cues.text: In 2013 the United States Supreme Court decided Association for Molecular Pathology versus Myriad Genetics. Its holding: a naturally occurring DNA segment is a product of nature, and isolating it does not make it patent eligible.

Complementary DNA, cDNA, is different. Made from messenger RNA, it holds only the exons, a molecule that does not occur in nature, so it is patent eligible. The exception is a very short cDNA that has no introns to remove and so matches natural DNA.
The Court said what it did not decide: method claims, new applications of knowledge about the BRCA genes, and DNA whose natural nucleotide order has been altered.
This is United States law. Patent rules in other countries, including the Philippines, are not covered here.

props.label: US law only · Philippines not covered

scenes.title: Exosomes: sealed envelopes in body fluids
scenes.altText: Schematic vesicle: exosomes are small extracellular vesicles, typically about 30–150 nm, formed by the endosomal route (inward budding into multivesicular bodies, then release by exocytosis). Cargo card: mRNA, microRNA, lncRNA, proteins and lipids, protected by a lipid bilayer (DNA cargo is reported but disputed); found in almost all body fluids (plasma, urine, saliva, CSF and more). Study card (Taylor and Gercel-Taylor 2008): EpCAM-captured circulating tumour exosomes; levels of 8 diagnostic microRNAs were similar in tumour cells and exosomes; ovarian cancer exosomal microRNA profiles were distinct from benign disease; exosomal microRNA was not detected in normal controls. Caveat token: ISEV recommends the term “extracellular vesicles”; current methods enrich rather than purify exosomes. Hook answers card.

cues.text: Exosomes are small extracellular vesicles, typically about thirty to one hundred fifty nanometres, released from multivesicular bodies inside the cell.

They carry messenger RNA, microRNA, long non-coding RNA, proteins and lipids inside a protective lipid bilayer; whether they carry DNA is disputed. They are found in almost all body fluids, which makes them a liquid-biopsy source.

In a 2008 study, ovarian cancer patients’ exosomal microRNA profiles were distinct from those in benign disease, and exosomal microRNA was not detected in normal controls. The authors proposed it as a potential diagnostic marker. Naming and isolation methods still vary.

Hook answers: the drug-dosing chip has a clear precedent. A natural BRCA1 sequence cannot be patented in the United States just because it was isolated. Exosome microRNA is a promising research marker, not yet an established screening test.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Isolating a gene makes it patentable” (✓ Myriad 2013: isolated natural DNA is a product of nature; cDNA is patent eligible); “AmpliChip measures gene expression” (✓ it genotypes CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 for drug metabolism); “Exosome microRNA is an established ovarian cancer screening test” (✓ a 2008 study proposed it as a potential marker).

cues.text: Trap one: isolating a gene makes it patentable. No: isolated natural DNA is still a product of nature. It is cDNA that is patent eligible.
Trap two: the AmpliChip measures gene expression. No: it genotypes CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 to predict drug metabolism.
Trap three: exosome microRNA is an established screening test. No: it was proposed as a potential marker and is still being studied.

scenes.title: Recipe, remix, envelope
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Nature’s RECIPE (genomic DNA) can’t be owned just by copying it out; your REMIX (cDNA, exons only) can. The first chip read the body’s drug-processing recipe (CYP2D6, CYP2C19). Exosomes are sealed ENVELOPES posted into almost every body fluid, carrying RNA messages.” Tokens: recipe = natural DNA · remix = cDNA · envelope = exosome. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: nature’s recipe, genomic DNA, cannot be owned just by copying it out; your remix, exons-only cDNA, can. The first chip read the drug-processing recipe. Exosomes are sealed envelopes posted into almost every body fluid, carrying RNA messages.

Where it breaks: a very short cDNA can be identical to natural DNA; the ruling is United States law only; and exosome size, naming and isolation are not standardised, so a sample of envelopes may include other vesicles too.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Very short cDNA can equal natural DNA

scenes.altText: Two tokens: “First clinical microarray: AmpliChip = CYP2D6 + CYP2C19 genotyping · Myriad 2013: natural DNA no, cDNA yes (US)”, “Exosomes ~30–150 nm, lipid-enclosed, RNA cargo → liquid-biopsy research marker”.

cues.text: The first clinical microarray genotyped CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 for drug dosing, the 2013 Myriad ruling held that isolated natural DNA is not patent eligible in the United States but cDNA is, and exosomes are small lipid-enclosed vesicles whose microRNA cargo is being studied as a liquid-biopsy marker.

props.label: AmpliChip = CYP2D6 + CYP2C19 · Myriad: natural DNA no, cDNA yes (US)
Exosomes ~30–150 nm · RNA cargo · liquid-biopsy research

explanation.what: Plain language: the first microarray used routinely in patients read two genes that control how fast people break down many drugs. In 2013 the US Supreme Court said you cannot patent a natural gene just by pulling it out of the chromosome, but you can patent a lab-made exons-only copy (cDNA). Exosomes are tiny bubbles cells release into blood and other fluids, carrying RNA and protein that may reveal disease. Scientific terms: oligonucleotide microarray, CYP2D6, CYP2C19, metaboliser phenotype, copy-number variation, product of nature, patent eligibility (35 USC 101), cDNA, extracellular vesicle, multivesicular body, microRNA, liquid biopsy.
explanation.why: Microarrays moved from research to diagnostics through pharmacogenetics; gene patents shaped who could offer genetic tests; exosomes protect their nucleic-acid cargo in a lipid bilayer and are present in almost all body fluids, which makes them attractive for noninvasive testing.
explanation.measure: AmpliChip: PCR, labelling, hybridisation, scanning, software phenotype prediction; does not give the exact number of extra CYP2D6 copies. Myriad: natural DNA not patent eligible merely because isolated; cDNA eligible except very short cDNA identical to natural DNA; method claims, applications and altered sequences not decided. Exosomes: about 30–150 nm (some sources 50–150 nm); mRNA, miRNA, lncRNA, proteins, lipids (DNA cargo disputed).
explanation.differs: Genotyping chip (AmpliChip) vs expression-profiling chip (such as MammaPrint); isolated natural DNA vs cDNA; exosomes vs cell-free DNA; research marker vs established screening test.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: name the first clinical microarray and its genes, decide whether isolated DNA or cDNA is patent eligible after Myriad, or recognise exosomes and their cargo as a liquid-biopsy source.

questions.stem: Under the 2013 US Supreme Court decision in AMP v. Myriad Genetics, which of the following is patent eligible?

options.text: A cDNA copy of the BRCA1 coding sequence made from mRNA
options.rationale: Correct. cDNA is an exons-only molecule that does not occur naturally, so the Court held it patent eligible (except very short cDNA identical to natural DNA).

options.text: An isolated, naturally occurring BRCA1 genomic DNA segment
options.rationale: Incorrect. A naturally occurring DNA segment is a product of nature and is not patent eligible merely because it has been isolated.

options.text: The discovered location and sequence of the BRCA1 gene
options.rationale: Incorrect. Discovering where a gene is and what its sequence is did not create or alter the genetic information, so it is not patent eligible.

options.text: A natural BRCA1 fragment cut from the chromosome by breaking its chemical bonds
options.rationale: Incorrect. The Court rejected the argument that severing bonds to isolate DNA makes it a new, patent-eligible molecule.

questions.stem: The Roche AmpliChip CYP450 test, described as the first clinically available microarray-based test, analyses which of the following?

options.text: CYP2D6 and CYP2C19 genotypes, to predict drug-metabolising phenotype
options.rationale: Correct. It is an oligonucleotide microarray that genotypes these two cytochrome P450 genes and predicts metaboliser phenotype.

options.text: Expression of 70 genes to predict breast cancer recurrence
options.rationale: Incorrect. That describes MammaPrint, an expression-profiling microarray test.

options.text: The exact number of extra CYP2D6 gene copies in every patient
options.rationale: Incorrect. The test detects duplications but does not determine the exact number of extra copies.

options.text: MicroRNA profiles of circulating tumour exosomes
options.rationale: Incorrect. Exosomal microRNA profiling is a research approach, unrelated to the AmpliChip.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes exosomes as a liquid-biopsy source?

options.text: Small lipid-bilayer vesicles, about 30–150 nm, carrying nucleic acids and proteins and found in most body fluids
options.rationale: Correct. Exosomes form via multivesicular bodies, carry mRNA, microRNA, lncRNA, proteins and lipids (DNA cargo is disputed), and occur in almost all body fluids.

options.text: Naked DNA fragments circulating without any membrane
options.rationale: Incorrect. Exosomes are membrane vesicles: their cargo is enclosed by a lipid bilayer, not free in the plasma.

options.text: Intact circulating tumour cells captured from blood
options.rationale: Incorrect. Circulating tumour cells are whole cells, a different liquid-biopsy analyte.

options.text: A validated, routine screening test for ovarian cancer
options.rationale: Incorrect. A 2008 study proposed exosomal microRNA as a potential marker; it is not an established screening test.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 70 Hit 3 states the AMP v. Myriad (2013) holding without jurisdiction or limits. It is a US Supreme Court decision; the opinion also excludes very short cDNA indistinguishable from natural DNA and leaves method claims, new applications and altered sequences undecided. Philippine patent rules are not covered (register flag rv-myriad-us-scope).

Ch. 70 Hit 14 gives exosomes as 30–150 nm and ovarian cancer exosomal miRNA as absent in normal controls. Size bands vary between sources (Doyle 2019 gives both 30–150 and 50–150 nm), ISEV recommends the umbrella term “extracellular vesicles”, current methods enrich rather than purify exosomes (Zhou 2020), and the normal-control finding comes from a single 2008 study (Taylor 2008; register flag rv-exosome-definition-evidence).

Ch. 70 Hit 2 calls the AmpliChip the first microarray cleared as a diagnostic device. Reviews agree it was first, but word it differently (first FDA-approved pharmacogenetic test; first clinically available microarray tool) and give the approval year as 2004 or 2005; the FDA 510(k) record could not be retrieved in this session.
